Mr Woodbury's published schedule cannot spend the money his own reform frees. It pays only on property tax above 4% of a household's income, and too little tax sits above that line: at his brackets the schedule spends $157.3 million of the $477.4 million available. The schedule modeled here keeps the shape of his proposal, a State share that rises as the burden rises, but starts the bands lower so that the freed funds are spent.

Above 4% Homestead Plus pays a smaller share of the tax than current law does, but it has no benefit base and no maximum credit, so households with the largest bills relative to their incomes receive considerably more. 18.title: Expand the Fairness Credit and Raise the Exemption to $35,000

full.html: Scenario 18 raises almost the same amount as Scenario 17 and spends it the other way round. Three quarters goes to the Fairness Credit and a quarter to the Homestead Exemption, which rises to $35,000. It is funded in the same way, by cutting the reimbursement rate to 50% and taking $73.0 million out of Revenue-Sharing I:

full.html: The two cuts raise $103.6 million: $73.0 million from Revenue-Sharing I and $30.6 million from the lower reimbursement rate, at the higher mill rates the scenario brings. Because the exemption rises only to $35,000 while the reimbursement rate halves, the State's homestead reimbursement bill ends up $3.4 million below what it pays today, so $73.8 million is free to expand the Fairness Credit, more than in any other scenario here except Scenario 19, which replaces the credit. A further $2.7 million is absorbed by the business equipment reimbursement.

The exemption adds $10,000 to the $25,000 already available. The maximum credit rises by 150%, to $3,750 and $5,000, and the benefit bases by 43%, both the largest increases among the four scenarios that keep today's credit formula. The Fairness Credit is aimed by income in a way the exemption is not, so spending the money this way concentrates it on the households paying the most property tax relative to what they earn. The burden threshold stays at 4.00%.
Scenario 17 moves a similar amount of money, about $100 million, and splits it evenly between the two programs instead, doubling the exemption rather than the credit.

Mill rates rise 0.48 mills statewide, or +3.43%, less than in Scenario 17 because a $35,000 exemption takes less value off municipal tax rolls than a $50,000 one. The scenario delivers $63.8 million of relief and cuts the number of households paying more than 6% of their income in property tax from 59,103 to 27,738, a reduction of 53% and the deepest cut of these five. The first decile gains $238 a household, more than the first decile gains in any other scenario here, and 54% of the relief reaches the bottom three deciles. The top two deciles lose on average, by $42 and $83. The Aroostook, Washington and northern Penobscot area receives 4.8% of the relief against 9.0% of Maine's households, roughly half its share.

19.title: Replace the Fairness Credit with a Two-Tier Credit and Double the Exemption

full.html: Scenario 19 was designed by Dick Woodbury, a member of the Task Force, and it is the only one here that changes the shape of the Fairness Credit rather than its size. At present the credit meets property tax above 4% of income in full, up to a maximum that depends on the claimant's age and household size. Under this scenario it meets the first $2,000 above that threshold in full and half of everything beyond, up to $5,000, and a single benefit base of $8,000 applies to every household whatever its age or size. The Homestead Exemption doubles alongside it, funded by cutting the reimbursement rate to 50% and taking $129.4 million out of Revenue-Sharing I:

full.html: The two cuts raise $161.0 million, half as much again as any other scenario here: $129.4 million from Revenue-Sharing I and $31.6 million from the lower reimbursement rate, at the higher mill rates the scenario brings. Of that, $90.5 million pays for the restructured credit, $65.9 million pays the State's reimbursement on the doubled exemption, and $4.6 million is absorbed by the business equipment reimbursement.

The revenue sharing cut is larger than it first appears it needs to be. Raising mill rates increases both the reimbursement the State owes on exempt homestead and business value and the credit it pays, because the credit is calculated from the property tax bill. Covering a $111.5 million shortfall therefore takes $129.4 million out of Revenue-Sharing I.

The exemption doubles, adding $25,000 to the $25,000 already available. The single $8,000 benefit base is the substantive change on the credit side. Four bases that rise with household size and two maximums that turn on age are replaced by one base and one schedule, so a household's entitlement depends on how large its property tax is relative to its income and on nothing else. The 50% second tier keeps the credit paying out well past the point at which the present one stops, and the maximum of $5,000 binds exactly where the benefit base does, since $2,000 plus half of the remaining $6,000 is $5,000. The burden threshold stays at 4.00%.

Mill rates rise 0.82 mills statewide, or +5.95%, the largest increase here, because this is both the largest revenue sharing cut and a doubled exemption. The scenario delivers $107.2 million of relief, also the largest, and cuts the number of households paying more than 6% of their income in property tax from 59,103 to 30,496, a reduction of 48%. Only the top decile loses on average, by $68 a household. The shape of the relief is unlike the others: it peaks at the seventh decile, at $286 a household, rather than the first, because a flat $8,000 base and a tapering second tier keep paying out for middle-income owners whose property tax is large relative to their income. The Aroostook, Washington and northern Penobscot area receives 7.3% of the relief against 9.0% of Maine's households.

intro.html: Archetype R1 includes homeowners with at least one dependent living at home. There are 117,460 such households, just over a quarter of all Maine homeowners, making this the second largest of the six Representative Archetypes.

The median householder in this archetype is 43. Median income is $119,600 and the median home is worth $319,000. They are overrepresented on the southern coast, where 36% of them live against a statewide 31%.

Their median property tax bill of $3,160 sits close to the state median, but their incomes are the highest of any archetype, so their median burden is the lightest of the owner archetypes bar one, at 2.7% of income. Fewer than one in five qualifies for the Fairness Credit.

vignette.html: Nathan and Erin Caouette live in New Gloucester with their children Charlotte, 11, and Will, 8. Nathan manages installations for a building-supply company in Gray; Erin is a physical therapist and works four days a week.

Between them they bring in $126,700. Their house is worth $338,000, and after the $25,000 homestead exemption New Gloucester's full-value rate of 11.47 mills puts their bill at $3,580, which is 2.8% of what they earn. The exemption saves them $290 a year.
They receive nothing from the Fairness Credit, because their income is too high for it to reach them: 4% of what they earn already exceeds the most property tax the credit will consider.

intro.html: Archetype R2 contains typical retirees: homeowners aged 65 or over with no dependents at home and income of $45,000 or more. There are 101,930 such households, 23% of all Maine homeowners.

The median householder in this archetype is 72. Median income is $88,300 and the median home is worth $309,000. They are overrepresented on the southern coast and in rural Maine, with 36% in each against a statewide 31% and 34%.

Their median property tax bill of $3,150 is indistinguishable from the state median, but their incomes are lower than those of working-age owners, so their median burden is higher at 3.3% of income. Just under a third qualify for the Fairness Credit, and the median claimant receives $910.

vignette.html: Paul and Diane Thibodeau, 72 and 70, have lived in the same house in Cushing since 1994. Paul ran a marine repair shop in Thomaston until he sold it; Diane taught third grade in the regional school unit.

With pensions and Social Security their income is $92,800. The house, a mile up from the river, is worth $319,000, and at Cushing's 10.75 mills their bill after the homestead exemption comes to $3,160, or 3.4% of income. The exemption is worth $270 a year.
They do not qualify for the Fairness Credit, because their property tax is already below 4% of their income, which is the point at which the credit begins to pay.

intro.html: Archetype R3 includes homeowners under 65 with no dependents at home and income of $45,000 or more. At 136,230 households, 31% of all Maine homeowners, this is the largest of the six Representative Archetypes.

It holds two kinds of household: working-age empty nesters whose children have grown up and left, and younger households without children. Two thirds of the archetype is aged 50 to 64 and only one in five is under 40. The median householder in this archetype is 55, median income is $111,000 and the median home is worth $301,000. They are spread more evenly across Maine than any other archetype, sitting within a couple of points of the statewide share in every region.

Their median property tax bill of $3,040 is close to the state median, but their incomes are the second highest of any archetype, so they carry the lightest median burden of any group at 2.5% of income. Only about one in nine qualifies for the Fairness Credit, and of those who do, three quarters are limited by the benefit base rather than by the maximum credit, which is another way of saying their bills are modest relative to what the program would pay.

vignette.html: Scott and Maureen Daigle are 55 and 54 and live in Manchester, a few miles west of Augusta. Scott is a civil engineer with the Department of Transportation; Maureen manages scheduling for a hospital group. Their daughter finished college two years ago.
Together they earn $119,300. The house is worth $307,000, and at Manchester's 11.43 mills their post-exemption bill is $3,220, or 2.7% of income, with the exemption saving them $290.
They do not qualify for the Fairness Credit: their income is high enough that 4% of it exceeds their entire property tax bill.

intro.html: Archetype R4 includes homeowners with no dependents at home and income under $45,000. There are 88,400 such households, 20% of all Maine homeowners. It is the counterpart to Archetypes R2 and R3, which take the same households but with incomes above $45,000.

The median householder in this archetype is 68. Median income is $26,400 and the median home is worth $193,000. They are the most rural group in Maine, with nearly half living in rural areas compared to one-third of Mainers overall.

This is where today's relief does its work. Their median property tax bill of $1,910 is the smallest of the owner archetypes, but their incomes are far lower, so their median burden before relief is 7.6% of income, the highest of the six. Three quarters of them qualify for the Fairness Credit, the median claimant receives $1,380, and the archetype collects $55.5 million of current relief, more than any other. Their burden falls to exactly 4.0% of income.

That 4.0% is a feature of the Fairness Credit formula: a household that does not hit the maximum credit receives exactly the credit required to reduce its property tax burden to 4% of income. That is what happens to most households in this archetype that claim the credit. The maximum stops the other 39% short, so they remain above 4%.

vignette.html: Linda Michaud is 67 and has lived alone in Canaan since her husband died six years ago. She spent twenty-two years on the line at a shoe plant in Skowhegan and then twelve in a school kitchen.

Social Security and a small pension come to $27,000. The house is worth $200,000, and at Canaan's 10.60 mills her bill after the homestead exemption is $1,860, which is 6.9% of her income before any credit. The exemption saves her $270 a year.

She qualifies for the Fairness Credit, and because her bill sits below her benefit base and her credit below the maximum, the credit pays the whole of her tax above 4% of income and leaves her at exactly 4%.

intro.html: Archetype R5 includes all renting households headed by someone under 65. There are 117,410 such households, 77% of all Maine renters. Renters receive no property tax bill, so Maine treats 15% of their rent as property tax for the purposes of the Fairness Credit, on the reasoning that rent includes the landlord's tax. Every renter figure here uses that convention.

The median householder in this archetype is 38. Median income is $50,400 and median counted property tax is $1,800. They are the most urban of the Representative Archetypes, with 19% in Greater Portland against a statewide 9% and 32% in the service centers against 26%.

Their median burden is 3.5% of income, higher than any of the owner archetypes except the lower-income group. Just under two fifths qualify for the Fairness Credit, and the median claimant receives $650.

vignette.html: Katie and Ryan rent the upstairs of a two-family house in Eddington, across the river from Brewer. Katie is 39 and a part-time dental hygienist; Ryan drives for a freight company out of Bangor.
Their combined income is $56,200 and their contract rent is $980 a month. Under the statute, 15% of that rent, $1,760 a year, counts as property tax paid, which is 3.1% of their income.
They receive no credit, because 4% of their income is more than the whole of that counted amount.

intro.html: Archetype R6 includes all renting households headed by someone aged 65 or over. There are 35,740 such households, 23% of all Maine renters, making this the smallest of the six Representative Archetypes.

The median householder in this archetype is 75. Median income is $27,300 and median counted property tax is $1,210. They are more urban than the state as a whole, with 13% in Greater Portland against a statewide 9%, and close to the statewide share everywhere else.

Their median burden is 3.9% of income. Nearly half qualify for the Fairness Credit, the median claimant receives $550, and the credit does more for them than for any other Representative Archetype: the share with a property tax burden above 4% of income falls from 47% to 3%.

vignette.html: Arlene is 75 and rents a one-bedroom in Mechanic Falls, a few streets up from the old mill. She worked in the office of a trucking firm in Auburn for most of her life.

Social Security and a small annuity give her $28,800 a year, and her rent is $900 a month. 15% of that, $1,620, counts towards the Fairness Credit, making up 5.6% of her income before the credit is applied.
After receiving a Fairness Credit of $460, her burden is exactly 4.0% of her income.

intro.html: Archetype B1 contains burdened retirees: homeowners aged 65 or over who live alone, have no dependents, own a home worth under $1,000,000, and still pay more than 6% of their income in property tax after all existing relief. There are 9,710 such households, 16% of all burdened households and 2% of all Maine homeowners.

The median householder in this archetype is 75. Median income is $25,800 and the median home is worth $405,000. They are overrepresented on the southern coast, where 39% of them live against a statewide 31%.

This is the most burdened archetype in Maine. Their median property tax bill is $5,400 and their median burden is 19.6% of income before any credit, ahead of every other group. Almost all of them qualify for the Fairness Credit, the median claimant already draws the full $2,000 senior maximum, and their median burden is still 10.7% of income after claiming it.
86% of claimants here are at the maximum credit. Increasing the benefit base or lowering the burden threshold will not help them; only a higher maximum credit does.

vignette.html: Pauline Beal is 76 and has lived in the same house in Milbridge for forty-one years. She worked in a blueberry processing plant and later kept the books for a wreath company. Her husband died in 2011.

Social Security and a small survivor pension come to $23,300 a year. The house, bought decades ago, is now worth $375,000. At Milbridge's 13.16 mills her bill after the homestead exemption is $4,610, which is nearly a fifth of her income, even after the exemption saves her $330.

She receives the maximum credit of $2,000, meaning her after-tax burden is 11.2% of her income. Without that maximum the formula would pay her $3,270 and leave her at 5.7%, so it is the cap that prevents her burden from falling further.

intro.html: Archetype B2 contains burdened retiree couples: homeowners aged 65 or over with no dependents, in a home worth under $1,000,000, who still pay more than 6% of their income in property tax after all existing relief. There are 10,090 such households, 17% of all burdened households and 2% of all Maine homeowners.
The median householder in this archetype is 72, in a home worth $493,000. They are overrepresented on the southern coast, where 40% of them live against a statewide 31%.

Their median property tax bill is $6,970, one of the largest of any archetype, but because their median income is $61,900, their typical property tax burden is around 12% of their income before relief, and around 9% after.
Just over half of claimants here are at the maximum credit and the rest are limited by the benefit base, so this archetype can be assisted through either lever.

vignette.html: Gordon and Nancy Leclerc are 73 and 71 and live in Cumberland, in a house they bought in 1988 when Gordon was still working for a paper company. Nancy worked in admissions at a community college.

Their pensions and Social Security come to $65,400. The house is worth $486,000, four times what they paid. At Cumberland's 14.88 mills their bill (after a $370 reduction due to the homestead exemption) is $6,860, or 10.5% of their income.

They receive a Fairness Credit of $1,580, bringing their burden to 8.1% of income. What prevents them from receiving further relief is the benefit base: the Fairness Credit only considers $4,200 of their tax bill, so increasing the maximum credit would not actually help them.

intro.html: Archetype B3 contains burdened single homeowners of working age: homeowners under 65 who live alone, have no dependents, own a home worth under $1,000,000, and still pay more than 6% of their income in property tax after all existing relief. There are 10,330 such households, 17% of all burdened households and 2% of all Maine homeowners.

The median householder in this archetype is 56, in a home worth $338,000. They are the most urban of the burdened owner archetypes, with 16% in Greater Portland against a statewide 9%, and are overrepresented on the southern coast at 38% against 31% statewide.

Their median income is $36,700 and their median property tax bill is $4,560, giving a median burden of 13.1% of income before relief and 9.3% after. Just under half of claimants here are at the maximum credit, and the median claimant receives $1,410.

vignette.html: Marc Bisson is 55 and lives by himself in Biddeford, in the house he kept after his divorce eleven years ago. He is a maintenance supervisor at a hospital.
His income is $33,500. The house is worth $375,000, and at Biddeford's 14.22 mills his bill (after a $360 reduction due to the homestead exemption) is $4,980, or 14.9% of his income.

He receives a Fairness Credit of $1,260, bringing his burden to 11.1% of income. At 55 his benefit base is $2,600, so the Fairness Credit considers only $2,600 of his tax bill. Were he ten years older, the same house and the same income would bring him the senior maximum credit of $2,000.

B4.title: Working-age owner, lives with a partner

intro.html: Archetype B4 contains burdened working-age couples: homeowners under 65 who live with a partner, have no dependents, own a home worth under $1,000,000, and still pay more than 6% of their income in property tax after all existing relief. There are 8,840 such households, 15% of all burdened households and 2% of all Maine homeowners.
The median householder in this archetype is 58, in a home worth $437,000. They are overrepresented on the southern coast, where 42% of them live against 31% statewide.

Their median income is $67,400, among the highest of the burdened owner archetypes, and their median property tax bill is $6,380. That gives them the mildest median burden of any burdened owner archetype, 9.9% of income before relief and 8.0% after. Just under two thirds qualify for the Fairness Credit, and the median claimant receives $1,230.
42% of claimants here are at the maximum credit, the lowest share of any burdened owner archetype, so this group is limited mainly by the benefit base rather than by the maximum.

vignette.html: Bruce and Carol Verrill are 63 and 61 and have been in their house in Yarmouth for nineteen years. Bruce is a parts manager for a boatyard; Carol does medical billing from home and has cut back to three days. Their two sons have long since moved out.
Together they make $69,300. The house is worth $429,000, and at Yarmouth's 16.17 mills their bill (after a $400 reduction due to the homestead exemption) is $6,530, or 9.4% of their income.

They receive a Fairness Credit of $580, bringing their burden to 8.6% of income. Bruce plans to stop working at 66. When he does, their income will fall by about a third and their tax bill will not change at all.

intro.html: Archetype B5 contains burdened families with children: homeowners with at least one dependent at home who still pay more than 6% of their income in property tax after all existing relief. There are 9,460 such households, 16% of all burdened households and 2% of all Maine homeowners.

The median householder in this archetype is 44, in a home worth $486,000. They are the newest to their homes of any burdened owner archetype, with 36% having moved within the last four years. They are overrepresented on the southern coast, where 42% of them live against 31% statewide.

Their median income is $73,300, the second highest of the burdened owner archetypes, and their median property tax bill is $6,980. Their median burden is 10.3% of income before relief and 8.4% after. Two thirds qualify for the Fairness Credit, and the median claimant receives the full $1,500 maximum available to a household under 65.

58% of claimants here are at the maximum credit, the highest share of the working-age owner archetypes. Their dependents give them the largest benefit base available to a household under 65, which is why their burden after relief sits below that of Archetype B1 despite a much larger tax bill.

vignette.html: Jason and Melissa Hanscom are 45 and 43 and live in South Berwick with their children Owen, 14, and Ruby, 11. Jason is a project estimator for a contractor in Portsmouth; Melissa is an educational technician at the elementary school and does bookkeeping in the evenings. They bought the house in 2019, at the top of what they could manage.

Their household income is $70,400. The house is worth $579,000, and at South Berwick's 13.42 mills their bill (after a $340 reduction due to the homestead exemption) is $7,440, or 10.6% of their income.

They receive a Fairness Credit of $1,330, bringing their burden to 8.7% of income. Their two dependents give them a benefit base of $4,150, the highest available to a household under 65, and it still covers only a little over half of their tax bill.

intro.html: Archetype B6 contains burdened owners of high-value homes: homeowners with no dependents in a home worth $1,000,000 or more who still pay more than 6% of their income in property tax after all existing relief. There are 4,530 such households, 8% of all burdened households and 1% of all Maine homeowners, making this the smallest archetype in the tool.
The median householder in this archetype is 68, in a home worth $1,500,000. 57% of them live on the southern coast, nearly twice the statewide share.

What places these households among the burdened is the value of their homes rather than a shortage of income. Their median income of $92,800 is the highest of any burdened archetype, and half of them sit in the top four income deciles, a larger share than any other burdened archetype. But their median property tax bill is $10,810, also the highest, and a bill that size carries a household past 6% of income even on an income like that.

Their median burden is 11.8% of income before relief and 10.8% after, the smallest movement of any burdened archetype. Only half qualify for the Fairness Credit, the rest are disqualified by their income. For those who do qualify, the maximum credit binds long before their bill is reduced anywhere near 4% of their income.

vignette.html: Peter and Susan Chadbourne are 66 and 64 and live in Cornish, in a house on land that has been in Susan's family since the 1940s. Peter sold his insurance agency some years ago; between drawdowns, Social Security and what the land brings in they report $92,800 a year.

The property is assessed at $1,300,000. Cornish's full-value rate is just 7.82 mills, about half the statewide average, because a town with very valuable property can raise what it needs at a lower rate. Their bill still comes to $9,970, and the homestead exemption is worth only $200 to them. That is 10.7% of their income.

They receive a Fairness Credit of $490, which lowers their burden from 10.7% to 10.2% of income. What limits them is the benefit base: the Fairness Credit will consider only $4,200 of their $9,970 bill, and 4% of their income consumes all but $490 of that.

intro.html: Archetype B7 contains burdened renters: renting households of any age whose counted property tax, being 15% of their rent, still exceeds 6% of their income after all existing relief. There are 6,150 such households, 10% of all burdened households and 4% of all Maine renters.
The median householder in this archetype is 32, the youngest of any archetype. They are overwhelmingly urban: 47% of them live in Greater Portland, five times the statewide share.

Their median income is $18,300, the lowest of any archetype, and 15% of their rent counts as $3,280 of property tax. Their median burden is 16.7% of income before relief and 8.6% after, the largest proportional fall of any burdened archetype. Almost all of them qualify for the Fairness Credit, and the median claimant receives the full $1,500 maximum available to a household under 65.
77% of claimants here are at the maximum credit, second only to B1, so this group is limited chiefly by the maximum rather than by the benefit base.

These figures should be read with one caution. 63% of this archetype reports annual rent above its annual income, which happens in survey data when income is understated or when a household is drawing on savings, family support or arrears. Their burdens are therefore likely to be overstated.

vignette.html: Denise Ouellette is 46 and rents a one-bedroom in Westbrook, where she has lived for seven years. She works split shifts as a home health aide and picks up weekend hours when they are offered.
Her income last year was $25,700 and her rent is $1,700 a month. 15% of that rent, $3,060, counts towards the Fairness Credit, making up 11.9% of her income before the credit is applied.

She receives the maximum credit of $1,500, which brings her burden down to 6.1% of her income. Two limits keep her above 4%: the Fairness Credit considers only $2,600 of the $3,060 counted, and even that is then capped at $1,500.

The median householder in this archetype is 75, median income is $27,300 and median counted property tax is $1,210.

Their median burden is 3.9% of income. Nearly half qualify for the Fairness Credit, the median claimant receives $550, and the credit lifts them further than it lifts any other Representative Archetype: the share with a burden above 4% of income falls from 47% to 3%.

B1.html: Archetype B1 contains burdened retirees: homeowners aged 65 or over who live alone, have no dependents, own a home worth under $1,000,000, and still pay more than 6% of their income in property tax after all existing relief. There are 9,710 such households, 16% of all burdened households. The median householder in this archetype is 75, median income is $25,800 and the median home is worth $405,000.

This is the most burdened archetype in Maine. Their median property tax bill is $5,400 and their median burden is 19.6% of income before any credit. Almost all of them qualify for the Fairness Credit, but 86% of claimants are already at the maximum, so their median burden is still 10.7% after claiming it. Raising the benefit base or lowering the burden threshold will not reach them; only a higher maximum credit does.

B2.html: Archetype B2 contains burdened retiree couples: homeowners aged 65 or over with no dependents, in a home worth under $1,000,000, who still pay more than 6% of their income in property tax after all existing relief. There are 10,090 such households, 17% of all burdened households. The median householder in this archetype is 72, in a home worth $493,000. They are overrepresented on the southern coast, where 40% of them live against a statewide 31%.

Their median property tax bill is $6,970, one of the largest of any archetype, but because their median income is $61,900, their typical burden is around 12% of income before relief and around 9% after. Just over half of claimants are at the maximum credit and the rest are limited by the benefit base, so this archetype can be assisted through either lever.

B3.html: Archetype B3 contains burdened single homeowners of working age: homeowners under 65 who live alone, have no dependents, own a home worth under $1,000,000, and still pay more than 6% of their income in property tax after all existing relief. There are 10,330 such households, 17% of all burdened households. The median householder in this archetype is 56, in a home worth $338,000. They are the most urban of the burdened owner archetypes.

Their median income is $36,700 and their median property tax bill is $4,560, giving a median burden of 13.1% of income before relief and 9.3% after. Just under half of claimants are at the maximum credit, and the median claimant receives $1,410.

B4.html: Archetype B4 contains burdened working-age couples: homeowners under 65 who live with a partner, have no dependents, own a home worth under $1,000,000, and still pay more than 6% of their income in property tax after all existing relief. There are 8,840 such households, 15% of all burdened households. The median householder in this archetype is 58, in a home worth $437,000. They are overrepresented on the southern coast, where 42% of them live against 31% statewide.

Their median income is $67,400 and their median property tax bill is $6,380, giving them the mildest median burden of any burdened owner archetype, 9.9% of income before relief and 8.0% after. Just under two thirds qualify for the Fairness Credit. Only 42% of claimants are at the maximum credit, so this group is limited mainly by the benefit base.

B5.html: Archetype B5 contains burdened families with children: homeowners with at least one dependent at home who still pay more than 6% of their income in property tax after all existing relief. There are 9,460 such households, 16% of all burdened households. The median householder in this archetype is 44, in a home worth $486,000. They are the newest to their homes of any burdened owner archetype, with 36% having moved within the last four years.

Their median income is $73,300 and their median property tax bill is $6,980, giving a median burden of 10.3% of income before relief and 8.4% after. Two thirds qualify for the Fairness Credit, and the median claimant receives the full $1,500 maximum available to a household under 65. Their dependents give them the largest benefit base available under 65, so 58% of claimants are stopped by the maximum rather than the base.

B6.html: Archetype B6 contains burdened owners of high-value homes: homeowners with no dependents in a home worth $1,000,000 or more who still pay more than 6% of their income in property tax after all existing relief. There are 4,530 such households, 8% of all burdened households, making this the smallest archetype in the tool. The median householder in this archetype is 68, in a home worth $1,500,000. 57% of them live on the southern coast, nearly twice the statewide share.

What places these households among the burdened is the value of their homes rather than a shortage of income. Their median income of $92,800 is the highest of any burdened archetype, and half of them sit in the top four income deciles. But their median property tax bill is $10,810, also the highest, and a bill that size carries a household past 6% of income even on an income like that. Their median burden is 11.8% before relief and 10.8% after, the smallest movement of any burdened archetype. Only half qualify for the Fairness Credit, the rest disqualified by their income.

B7.html: Archetype B7 contains burdened renters: renting households of any age whose counted property tax, being 15% of their rent, still exceeds 6% of their income after all existing relief. There are 6,150 such households, 10% of all burdened households and 4% of all Maine renters. The median householder in this archetype is 32, the youngest of any archetype, and they are overwhelmingly urban: 47% of them live in Greater Portland, five times the statewide share.

Their median income is $18,300, the lowest of any archetype, and 15% of their rent counts as $3,280 of property tax. Their median burden is 16.7% of income before relief and 8.6% after, the largest proportional fall of any burdened archetype. Almost all of them qualify for the Fairness Credit and 77% of claimants are at the maximum, so this group is limited chiefly by the maximum rather than by the benefit base.

Scenarios.html: On this page you can explore 19 different scenarios, each of which represents a change to the way in which Maine provides property tax relief to households, and learn about how each scenario would affect households at different levels of income or in different parts of the state.
There are three distinct types of policy scenario:

items.html: 8 scenarios which spend $35 million of new State spending: These scenarios answer the following question: what are the different ways that the State of Maine could spend an extra $35 million more on expanding the existing property tax relief programs?

6 scenarios which reallocate money between existing relief programs: These scenarios are designed to be revenue-neutral: they leave overall State spending unchanged. Instead, they consider what could be achieved by abolishing one or more existing relief programs and directing all of the freed-up funds into expanding a different relief program.

5 Task Force scenarios: These were developed using guidance from Task Force deliberations (S15-S17), the Consultants’ own proposal (S18) and a Fairness Credit redesign proposed by one member of the Task Force (S19). These scenarios all involve revenue-neutral reallocations of funds away from municipal-level relief (Homestead Exemption reimbursement & Revenue-Sharing) and towards household-level relief (Homestead Exemption & Fairness Credit). They differ in the scale of funds reallocated (from $73.5 million to $161.0 million) and in how the funds are split between the Homestead Exemption and Fairness Credit. All of these scenarios result in mill rate increases as municipalities replace the funds reallocated away from municipal-level relief.

Scenarios:more.title: Learn more about Maine’s existing property tax relief programs

blocks.html: Maine helps households with their property tax in three main ways. The homestead exemption removes a fixed amount of value from the tax bill of anyone who owns and occupies their home, and the State reimburses municipalities for most of the revenue they give up by granting it. The Property Tax Fairness Credit pays money back to households whose property tax, or whose rent, is large relative to their income; it is claimed each year on a Maine income tax return. Municipal revenue sharing sends a share of State tax collections to municipalities, reducing what they must raise locally.

The nineteen scenarios on this page are possible changes to those three programs. Scenarios 1-3 expand the Homestead Exemption, Scenarios 4-8 expand the Fairness Credit, Scenarios 9-13 redirect the funds from other relief programs into the Fairness Credit, Scenario 14 replaces all existing forms of relief with a proposed new policy called ‘Homestead Plus’, and Scenarios 15-19 move funds from Revenue-Sharing I, and in four of them from the homestead reimbursement, into a larger Homestead Exemption and a larger Fairness Credit together.

Archetypes.html: While the Policy Scenarios tab displays statewide results for each of the modeled reforms, those results lump together many different types of household. On this page you can explore how changes to property tax relief affect common types of Maine households, which we refer to as Archetypes.
There are three distinct sets, built for different purposes:

items.html: The 6 Representative Archetypes are broadly-defined and familiar types of household: working-age renters, a family with children, empty-nesters, etc. Every single household in Maine is placed into one of these Representative Archetypes.

The 7 Burdened Archetypes cover only households who we classify as ‘burdened’, meaning that their property taxes (or 15% of their rent) still exceeds 6% of their income even after existing relief programs. These are the 60,000 households that the current system does not adequately reach.

The 6 Commercial Archetypes are vignettes representing common types of Maine commercial property: a storefront, a repair shop, a restaurant, a professional office, a lumber yard and a ten-unit apartment building. None of them receives the Homestead Exemption or the Fairness Credit, so the only way any scenario reaches them is through their municipality's mill rate.

Archetypes.html: Below you can learn more about each type of household: where they live and how much they typically earn, how their property tax burden is improved by existing relief programs, and how each of the policy scenarios would provide additional relief.

Each archetype includes a vignette, which describes the circumstances of a very typical example from within it. For the household archetypes, the names and occupations are made up but the finances are real: they represent survey data from a real household within the model. For the commercial archetypes, the premises are real parcels taken from municipal commitment books and described in general terms, so that no individual business can be identified; their tax bills are the ones their municipality actually billed, while the revenue and profit figures are rough industry estimates rather than anything reported by the business itself.

C1.label: A martial arts studio in Bangor

vignette.html: A karate and jiu-jitsu school on a side street a few minutes from downtown Bangor. Classes run from late afternoon into the evening, children first and adults after, and enrollment swells in January and thins out by July.

The school bought its building rather than renting, which is the ambition of most small operations like it and the reason this one is still in the same place after fifteen years. It has half an acre to itself and about 5,760 square feet, most of it one matted room, with changing rooms, a cramped office and a row of chairs along the wall where parents wait. The lot matters as much as the building: twenty minutes either side of each changeover the parking fills completely, and a dozen spaces of its own is the difference between a workable location and an impossible one.

A school this size takes somewhere around a quarter of a million dollars a year in tuition and clears perhaps $60,000 of that before the owner draws any pay. The city assesses the property at about $500,000, and at Bangor's rate of 17.7 mills the school pays $8,788 a year in property tax, the figure its commitment book shows was billed. That is one dollar in every twenty-eight that comes through the door, and roughly a quarter of everything the school spends on having a building at all.

C1.summary: Bill today $8,788. Clears roughly $60,000 a year before the owner draws pay.

C2.label: A repair shop in Gardiner

vignette.html: A three-bay garage on the commercial road into Gardiner, doing brakes, exhausts, tyres and state inspections. Two bays have lifts; the third is where the long jobs sit while a part comes up from Portland. There is a waiting room with a coffee machine and magazines a year out of date, and most of the work arrives by word of mouth from people who have been coming since the owner’s father ran it.

The shop takes in around $600,000 a year and clears about $57,000 of that after the owner has paid himself a wage and before income tax, which is the nine or ten cents on the dollar the trade typically returns. The town assesses the property at $275,000, and at Gardiner’s rate of 25.6 mills the shop pays $7,040 a year in property tax. That is a little over 1% of what comes through the door, and about an eighth of what the business keeps.

C2.summary: Bill today $7,040. Clears about $57,000 a year after the owner's wage.

C3.label: A restaurant in Camden

vignette.html: A seventy-seat restaurant a block from Camden harbor, in a commercial building put up around 1900 and converted to a dining room some decades later. Lunch and dinner through the season, dinner only once the leaf-peepers have gone, closed for a few weeks in March. Most of the year’s trade happens between the Fourth of July and the end of foliage, and the owner spends the winter working out how much of the kitchen staff can be kept on until spring.
The building is 2,444 square feet on a lot barely larger than its own footprint. There is no parking and no terrace, and deliveries come through the front door in the hour before service.

At the $250 to $325 per square foot that full-service restaurants typically take, a room this size turns over around $700,000 a year. Full-service restaurants clear three to five cents on the dollar after costs, so the business keeps somewhere between $25,000 and $35,000. The town assesses the property at just under $845,000, and at Camden's rate of 11.5 mills the restaurant pays $9,700 a year in property tax. That is about 1.4% of turnover, and close to a third of everything the business clears in a year.

C3.summary: Bill today $9,700. Clears somewhere between $25,000 and $35,000 a year.

vignette.html: A two-lawyer practice on Route 302 in Raymond, doing the work a lake town generates: camp and cottage closings through the summer, wills and estates all year, and the occasional boundary dispute between neighbors who have been arguing about the same stone wall since the 1970s. One of the partners sits as counsel to a neighboring town’s planning board.

The firm owns its building, a modest place set back from the highway on four tenths of an acre, with parking for clients at the door. Raymond’s commitment book records no floor area for the property, so the size of the building is not something the data can tell us.

A practice of this size bills perhaps half a million dollars a year, and in an owner-operated firm the partners’ own earnings are the profit. The town assesses the property at $310,500, and at Raymond’s rate of 17.2 mills the firm pays $5,341 a year in property tax, a little over 1% of what it bills.

A lumber and hardware yard in York, selling framing stock, sheet goods, trim, fasteners and paint to the builders who keep the town’s houses standing and its second homes renovated. Contractors come through before seven, homeowners after nine on Saturdays, and the counter staff know which of the regulars pay on time.

The yard sits on about an acre and three quarters: a covered store, racks of dimensional lumber under cover at the back, a trade counter at the front, and enough hardstanding for a delivery truck to turn around.

A yard this size turns over several million dollars a year, and the building materials trade runs on roughly four cents of net profit in the dollar, so the business keeps perhaps $200,000 of it. The town assesses the property at just under $1.2 million, and at York’s rate of 8.4 mills it pays $9,940 a year in property tax, which is the figure the commitment book shows was billed. That is a fifth of one per cent of sales, and about 5% of what the yard clears.

A ten-unit apartment complex on a residential street a few minutes from the center of Bangor. Three two-story buildings sit on just under an acre, four flats in one and three in each of the others, built in the mid-1980s and clad in vinyl siding. Each flat has two bedrooms and runs to about 950 square feet, with hot water baseboard heat and its own parking space. The tenants are a mix of working households and students, and turnover is steady rather than dramatic.

It is owned by a local investor through a limited liability company, which is how most buildings of this size in Maine are held. The current owner bought it in 2010, and the city's assessment has more than doubled since.

The ten flats gross somewhere around $117,000 a year in rent, at the roughly $980 a month a two-bedroom typically fetches in the Bangor area. The city assesses the property at $1,258,700, and at Bangor's rate of 17.70 mills the owner pays $22,279 a year in property tax, the figure the commitment book shows was billed. That is $2,228 per flat a year, or $186 a month, and a little under a fifth of everything the building collects in rent. After the tax and the other costs of running the place, it clears perhaps $60,000 to $70,000 a year before any mortgage.

R1: 117,000 households, one in five, mildly concentrated on the Southern Coast. Medians: $119,600 income, $319,000 home, $3,160 bill, 2.7% of income. 8% are burdened after today's relief, down from 14% before it.
Only 19% qualify for the Fairness Credit. Of those who do, a quarter sit at the maximum and a third at the benefit base, so neither credit lever has much purchase on the group as a whole.

Homestead changes reach them and credit changes largely do not. Cutting reimbursement to 50% to fund a much larger exemption [S3] gives $184 a household, against $63 from higher benefit bases [S4], which reaches only one household in eight.

Most of them pay more under reallocation. Under three of the five reallocations [S10, S11, S12] a clear majority pay more, and even ending Revenue Sharing I [S9] leaves 59% worse off for an average gain of $117.
Their best outcome is all three sources combined [S13], at $279 a household, which cuts their burdened share from 8% to 3%. Even then, 48% pay more than they do today.
R2: 102,000 households, one in six. Medians: $88,300 income, $309,000 home, $3,150 bill, 3.3% of income. 11% are burdened after relief, down from 22% before it.

A third qualify for the credit, and the typical claimant receives $910, well below the maximum. 36% are held by the benefit base and only 10% by the maximum, so the base does more for them than the maximum does.
The senior liability ceiling [S7] is the only $35 million option built for them. It gives $132 a household and cuts their burdened share from 11% to 6%, further than any other $35 million scenario.
A larger exemption helps broadly [S3, $173] but does little for burden, because it is worth the same whatever a household's income.

Reallocation treats them better than it treats R1 or R3. All three sources combined [S13] gives $468 with 62% gaining, and ending Revenue Sharing I [S9] gives $283 with 53% gaining. Their burdened share falls to 4% under both S13 and Homestead Plus [S14].
R3: 136,000 households, nearly one in four and the largest archetype. Medians: $111,000 income, $301,000 home, $3,040 bill, 2.5% of income, the lightest burden of any group.
Only 11% qualify for the credit, the lowest share of any archetype, and three quarters of those are held by the benefit base rather than the maximum.
The credit levers therefore barely reach them. A higher maximum credit [S5] gives $15 a household. Higher benefit bases [S4] give $94 and reach fewer than one in five.
The Homestead Exemption is their program: $198 under a 50% reimbursement with a much larger exemption [S3], $98 under a straightforward increase [S1].

They are the clearest losers from reallocation. Under S10, S11 and S12 more than three quarters pay more, and cutting the homestead reimbursement into the credit [S11] leaves them $3 worse off on average. Ending Revenue Sharing I [S9] and the two largest reallocations [S13, S14] leave them better off on average, by $65, $189 and $173, but a majority still pay more under all three.
R4: 88,000 households, one in seven, half of them rural. Medians: $26,400 income, $193,000 home, $1,910 bill, 4.0% of income after relief. 25% are burdened, down from 67% before relief, the largest reduction today's programs achieve for any representative archetype.
Three quarters qualify for the credit and 39% sit at the maximum, but for most of them the 4% threshold is the binding limit.
That is why homestead changes are partly clawed back. A smaller bill means a smaller credit, so a larger exemption [S1] gives only $69 a household, against $185 for doubling the maximum credit [S5].

What reaches them is anything that lifts the maximum or lowers the threshold: $185 [S5], $226 under the senior ceiling [S7], $330 from ending Revenue Sharing I [S9], $427 from all three sources combined [S13].

They are the one representative archetype that gains broadly from reallocation. Under S9 and S13, 79% gain and 16% lose, and S13 cuts their burdened share from 25% to 7%. Homestead Plus [S14] is the exception: half pay more and their burdened share falls only to 14%.
R5: 117,000 households, one in five, overrepresented in Greater Portland. Medians: $50,400 income, $1,800 of rent counted towards the credit, 3.5% of income. 5% are burdened, down from 21% before relief.
Homestead changes give them nothing at all [S1 to S3]. The exemption applies to owner-occupied homes, and mill rate changes are not assumed to pass through into rents.
Two in five qualify for the credit, so credit changes reach them, but modestly: $42 from a higher maximum [S5], $23 from higher benefit bases [S4].

Reallocation is where they gain, because all of the money goes through the credit: $197 from ending Revenue Sharing I [S9], $307 from all three combined [S13], $248 from Homestead Plus [S14]. No renter loses under any reallocation.
S13 removes their burden almost entirely, from 5% to under 1%.
R6: 36,000 households, the smallest representative archetype, slightly more urban. Medians: $27,300 income, $1,200 of rent counted towards the credit, 3.9% of income. Only 1% are burdened after relief, against 26% before it, proportionally the largest reduction today's relief achieves for any group.
Half qualify for the credit, and for most of them it already resolves the burden, so there is little left for a larger credit to do.
The pattern is the same as R5: homestead changes do nothing, credit changes help a little, and reallocation helps most, at $129 [S9] and $193 [S13].
Homestead Plus [S14] is the one scenario that leaves more of them burdened than today, at 3% against 1%, and 6% of them pay more.
B1: 9,700 households, half in Greater Portland and on the Southern Coast. Medians: $25,800 income, $405,500 home. Their burden is 19.6% of income before the credit, the heaviest of any archetype, and still 10.7% after it.

98% are eligible and 86% sit at the maximum credit. The credit is working and the burden remains, which is the central fact about this group. They gain only if the maximum rises; the benefit base does almost nothing for them.

The senior liability ceiling [S7] is transformative: a median gain of $1,020, and the share above 6% falls from 100% to 8%, the largest reduction any $35 million scenario achieves for any owner archetype.
A higher maximum credit [S5] and the hybrid [S6] both reach them, at around $600, leaving about 60% above 6%. Higher benefit bases alone [S4] give the median household nothing.

Among reallocations, all three sources combined [S13] gives $1,623 and leaves 16% above 6%. Homestead Plus [S14] gives $809 and leaves 52%. Homestead changes do almost nothing: a larger exemption [S1] leaves 93% above 6%.
B2: 10,100 households, often on the Southern Coast. Medians: $61,900 income, $493,000 home, burden 8.9% of income after relief.

The same age profile as B1 on 2.4 times the income, and a burden 7.7 points lighter before the credit. That contrast is the clearest evidence in the set that what drives burden among older owners is living alone rather than age itself.
Only half sit at the maximum, so the benefit base does as much work here as the maximum credit. Higher bases [S4] reach 51% of them.

The senior ceiling [S7] is again their best $35 million option, at $709, leaving 39% above 6%. The universal ceiling [S8] does much less, at $77, because for many of them its payment falls below the credit they already receive.
All three sources combined [S13] gives $1,798 and leaves 27% above 6%; Homestead Plus [S14] gives $1,563 and leaves 32%.
B3: 10,300 households, mostly urban. Medians: $36,700 income, $337,600 home, burden 9.3% of income after relief.

Too young for the senior benefit base or the senior ceiling, and with no dependent uplift, so both credit levers are set at their least generous for them. Age rather than wealth is what separates this group from B1.
The senior ceiling [S7] does nothing for them at all: 100% remain above 6%.
The universal ceiling [S8] is their best $35 million option, at $396, and the only one that moves them materially, leaving 48% above 6%.

Reallocation and Homestead Plus are close to equivalent here, at $1,167 [S13] and $1,171 [S14], leaving 33% and 36% above 6%. Homestead Plus does relatively well for them because it has no benefit base to limit what they can claim.
B4: 8,800 households, often on the Southern Coast. Medians: $67,400 income, $437,500 home, burden 8.0% of income after relief, the mildest of the burdened set.
Among the highest incomes of the burdened owner archetypes, so after B6 the fewest qualify, at 63%. They are in this set because the burdened group is not only the old and the poor.
Base-bound rather than cap-bound: 58% are held by the benefit base against 42% by the maximum. Higher bases [S4] give $315, nearly three times what a higher maximum gives [S5, $111].
Homestead Plus [S14] is their best outcome by a clear margin: $1,601, with 99% better off and 24% left above 6%, against $1,323 and 40% under all three sources combined [S13].
B5: 9,500 households, often on the Southern Coast. Medians: $73,300 income, $485,800 home, burden 8.4% of income after relief. The newest to their homes of any owner archetype: the median household moved in five to nine years ago and 36% within the last four years.
Their dependents lift their benefit base, which is why their post-credit burden lands below B1's despite a much larger bill. 58% sit at the maximum credit.
No $35 million scenario does much for them. The hybrid [S6] gives the most, a median $476, but leaves 82% above 6%; the universal ceiling [S8] leaves the fewest above 6%, at 76%.
Reallocation is where the change happens: $1,600 under all three sources combined [S13], leaving 33% above 6%, and $1,687 under Homestead Plus [S14], leaving 27%.
B6: 4,500 households, often on the Southern Coast. Medians: $92,800 income, $1.5m home, burden 10.8% of income after relief.
The largest bills of any archetype and the smallest share eligible of the burdened set, because income disqualifies about half of them.

The only burdened archetype whose burden barely moves after the credit, from 11.8% to 10.8%, because the maximum binds long before the bill does. They are burdened by the value of their home rather than by low income, which makes them both the case for a liability ceiling and the case against it.

The senior ceiling [S7] does the most for their burden of any $35 million option, cutting the share above 6% from 100% to 73%. The universal ceiling [S8] does nothing for them at all, because it counts only the first $370,000 of a home's value.
Even the largest reallocations leave most of them burdened: about $1,300 under both S13 and S14, with roughly 70% still above 6%.
B7: 6,100 households, often in Greater Portland. Median income $18,330, the lowest of any archetype. Burden 8.6% of income after relief.
93% are eligible, second only to B1, and 77% sit at the maximum credit. The credit does more work here than anywhere else, cutting their burden roughly in half.
Homestead changes do nothing at all [S1 to S3]: 100% remain above 6%.
The universal ceiling [S8] is the single most effective scenario for them of any on this page, cutting the share above 6% from 100% to 3%, provided renters are included in it.
All three sources combined [S13] leaves 7% above 6%; Homestead Plus [S14] leaves 27%.

Two cautions. A renter's "tax" is the statutory 15% of rent, a proxy rather than a bill anyone receives. And 63% of this group reports annual rent exceeding annual income, so cash income understates their resources and this burden figure is indicative rather than directly comparable with an owner's.
